# Redis, Leaderboards and Locking

## Category

database / cache subtree. Node position: boundary governance for cache, leaderboards and distributed locks — "who is fact, who is acceleration", plus the lease cost of locks. This page is the boundary outline of the cache subtree.

## Definition


Cache, leaderboards and distributed locks are often introduced as "performance accessories", but what they actually affect is the boundary line inside the system of "who is fact, who is acceleration". Redis is fast enough that many teams casually push more and more state into it, until one outage reveals that they have been writing authoritative data into a component that loses state on restart, switches primary/replica, and can fill its memory.

This page discusses three high-frequency facets: what cache should actually carry, why a leaderboard score is harder to design than the structure, and where the real cost of a distributed lock goes.

## Problem

All three are treated as "performance accessories" when adopted, and what they actually affect is the boundary of "who is fact, who is acceleration". The most expensive wrong ledgers all happen when the boundary is inverted: writing authoritative state into a component that loses state on restart, switches primary/replica, and runs out of memory, only to discover on outage day that restoring the cache is not the same as restoring the data; locks only narrow the concurrency window and do not provide correctness — if you only design the success path of acquiring the lock, the lease, contention and accidental deletion will all settle on the day traffic arrives.


### The positioning of cache: an acceleration layer, not a fact layer

The value of cache comes from one simple premise: the same data is read repeatedly, and computing or fetching it from the source once costs more. The point of cache existing is to make "reads fast", not to make "data live here". Once that premise is inverted — reading cache becomes a habit, and nobody can say clearly where the source is anymore — cache turns from an acceleration layer into the de facto authoritative store, without ever having been prepared for that role.

Whether a piece of data can go into cache usually comes down to these conditions:

- The source is explicit, and it can be rebuilt or recovered without relying on the cache.
- Short staleness is acceptable, and the staleness window is imperceptible to the business or compensable.
- Access frequency is high enough, otherwise the maintenance cost of caching cannot be recovered.
- Size is controllable, so it does not push memory pressure onto the whole cluster.

Of the four, the one most often ignored is the first. Hit rate, expiration, and eviction policy have plenty of existing discussion; "who is the source of this data" is very often left unanswered by anyone.

### Treating cache as the authoritative source — the cost is usually only settled on outage day

Use cache as the authoritative source day to day, and the monitoring curves barely show anything wrong: requests are fast, business is normal. The difference only shows the day Redis restarts, primary/replica switches, or memory eviction triggers — and at that point what is lost is not a cache entry, but a batch of state "that only exists in cache".

These incidents share a few features:

- Restoring the cache is not the same as restoring the data, because the source was never complete in the first place.
- The affected state is often scattered across several business lines, hard to fill in one by one afterwards.
- With no reconciliation mechanism, the team cannot even say how much was actually lost.

A more solid approach is to reverse the assumption: for any state written into cache, first answer "after the cache is emptied, where is this data rebuilt from". If the answer is "it cannot be rebuilt", it usually belongs in the persistence layer, with the cache holding only a replica; if the answer is "regenerated by replaying events", then confirm that the replay path actually exists and has been rehearsed.

### Why leaderboards usually land on sorted sets

A leaderboard's core operations are very stable: update some member's score, fetch the top N, look up some member's rank. A sorted set pushes the cost of all three operations down to logarithmic level, and it also handles the stable ordering of tied members, so it often becomes the default choice — and that choice is right most of the time.

But it is not the only option, and it does not cover every leaderboard shape. Common variant scenarios include:

- The board is enormous but only the top hundred are displayed; a snapshot produced by periodic aggregation is often cheaper.
- Multi-dimensional sorting or conditional filtering is needed, and a single sorted set's structure starts to distort.
- The board must merge across servers or switch by season, and member identity and lifecycle must be thought through first.

What deserves more attention at selection time is the leaderboard's lifecycle: when is the season board cleared, how are historical boards retained, how do read requests continue on the old board once a new one opens. These questions are more likely than "which structure to use" to be pushed until the night before launch.

### Score design is often harder than leaderboard structure

Structure selection is a ten-minute job; score semantics routinely come back for rework. The reason is that the "score" column has to carry sorting, tie-breaking and display all at once, and the business requirements on those three often conflict.

Problems that recur in practice are roughly these:

- Tied players' ranks are unstable, and refreshing the page makes the ranking jump.
- You want "whoever reached it first ranks higher" to break ties, but there is nowhere to record the time of achievement.
- The score must combine multiple dimensions, and concatenating them straight into a decimal quietly loses precision.
- Operations demands changing or zeroing scores, and only then is it discovered that the score field hides timestamps and dimension bits.

The common practice is to decide the tie-breaking rule up front: either accept tied ranks and guarantee stable ordering, or encode the achievement time into the low bits of the score. The former is simple but the display has to be self-consistent; the latter is easy, but tends to expose readability and precision problems once "the score has other uses". As a rule of thumb, once a score starts carrying metadata, it is worth splitting "displayed score" and "sort key" into two fields.

### How a leaderboard is read depends on rank or interval

On the same leaderboard, "show me the top ten" and "what rank am I" are two completely different kinds of read requests, an order of magnitude apart in cost. The top ten can be cached as a whole page and snapshotted periodically; looking up one's own rank is a separate request per player, hard to share, and therefore hard to cache.

Common handling ideas:

- Generate the head of the board periodically as a whole, and land all display-class requests on the snapshot.
- Provide a separate interface for personal rank, and make explicit the latency it is allowed.
- Prefer percentile or rank-tier conclusions over exact rank; the former can often be computed offline.

The root cause of many laggy leaderboards is every player checking their own rank in the same second an hourly event ends. At that point the problem is not the data structure — the read path was never designed.

### What problem does a distributed lock actually solve

A distributed lock's actual use is narrower than its frequency of appearance suggests: it solves the mutual exclusion problem of "multiple executors all believing it should be them" — for example a scheduled task that must run only once, a hot cache entry that must be filled from the source only once, the same order handled by only one consumer. It does not provide any strict correctness guarantee; it only narrows the concurrency window probabilistically.

Deciding whether to introduce a lock usually asks three questions:

- What is the cost of running this thing once more? Often the answer is harmless, and the lock can be dropped.
- What is done inside the locked critical section? Long operations that cross the network should not be here.
- What does the side that fails to get the lock do? Wait, give up, or degrade — this path is often never designed.

Of the three questions the most often skipped is the last one, and most of the online disputes around locks happen at the moment "someone did not get the lock".

### The real cost of locks: lease, clocks and renewal

A distributed lock has no true blocking, only leases. What the holder gets is a credential that expires, and once expired the lock becomes available to others again. So all the trouble grows out of that one point: "expiry". A lease too short and the lock lapses before the business finishes; a lease too long and after the holder crashes the system has to sit and wait a long time.

The common failure shapes are these:

- The business execution exceeds the lease duration, a second holder enters, and both sides write at the same time.
- Process pauses — garbage collection, virtual machine migration, disk stalls — leave the holder "believing it is still within the lease".
- At primary/replica switchover the lock record has not yet been replicated, and on the new primary the lock is in the released state.
- Releasing without verifying holder identity deletes the lock someone else just acquired.

The countermeasures also revolve around the lease: a renewal thread keeps long tasks alive, verify the credential before releasing and only then delete, and add a version check inside the critical section as the last line of defense. None of these layers is perfect; usually you decide how many layers of protection to stack by "the cost of the lock failing", and the higher the cost, the more worth stacking.

### Common pitfalls

- Treating Redis as storage that cannot lose anything, only to discover after a restart or a primary/replica switch that a batch of state has nowhere to be rebuilt.
- Packing timestamps and dimension bits into leaderboard scores, only to find they cannot be touched when operations asks to change a score.
- Designing only the success path of acquiring the lock, with no follow-up for lock contention, lock expiry or lock misdeletion.
- Using a lock to protect a long transaction that crosses the network, where the lease window cannot cover the critical section at all.

Problems with cache, leaderboards and locks rarely appear on adoption day; they tend to appear together on the day traffic rises, a node restarts, or operations changes the rules.

### Practical case: a lock lease investigation where "the compensation task ran twice and over-issued 6 million across the server"

> The case is a demonstration example (not drawn from a real project); the numbers are rounded for simplicity. It drives this page's "The positioning of cache: an acceleration layer, not a fact layer", "Treating cache as the authoritative source — the cost is usually only settled on outage day", "What problem does a distributed lock actually solve", "The real cost of locks: lease, clocks and renewal" and "Common pitfalls" into deep water: a single after-hours compensation run exposed at once the gap that "locks only narrow probability, they do not provide correctness" and the gap that "the list only lives in the cache".

**Background and symptoms**: A long-running project; operations demands re-issuing rewards to players affected by an event bug. The compensation script starts on schedule at **02**:**00** in the small hours: it walks the event participation list (during the event it was written directly into a Redis set for speed, and after the event nobody could say who the source should be) and calls the reward-issuance interface one by one, and the interface has no idempotency key. The task runs on machine A holding a **30**-minute lease; in the same window, machine B's compensation scheduler detects the lock is free and starts a task of the same name. Nobody notices anything wrong when the task window ends at **03**:**30**; at **04**:**10** the hourly reconciliation alert fires: the reward-issuance ledger's person-count is twice the list.

### Step 1: Symptoms and calibration — compute "how much should be issued" first, then look at "how much actually was"

Calibration aligned: "should be issued" is based on the compensation list (**500** gold per person); "actually issued" is based on the wallet service's reward-issuance ledger, reconciled on both person-count and amount. First record two entries:

- **Should be issued**: list of **12,000** people × **500** gold = **6,000,000**
- **Actually issued**: ledger of **24,000** person-entries, totaling **12,000,000** gold

Actual issuance is exactly twice what should have been issued — check the ledger distribution first, then work out the lock's account.

### Step 2: Layered attribution — the double-run ledger from reward-issuance ledger to lock lease

```text
名单账   补发名单 1.2 万人 × 500 金币 = 应发 600 万；发奖限速 200 人/分钟，全程 60 分钟
锁账     租约 30 分钟 < 任务 60 分钟：A 机 02:00 启动，02:30 租约到期未续期，B 机 02:30 抢到锁从头再跑
双跑账   两机各发一遍：流水 2.4 万人次 = 1.2 万 × 2，实发 1200 万，超发 600 万
对账账   以活动流水库重放出「每人 1 次」基准，核出 1.2 万人全部双发；回收 480 万（未消费 80%），已消费 120 万转活动对冲
```

The ledger closes: the task takes **60** minutes but the lease is only **30** minutes — a second holder is a **certainty**, not an accident; machine B restarted from the head of the list, and the reward-issuance interface had no idempotency key, so both runs took full effect. Being able to establish the facts depended on the event transaction database's replay path still existing — of this page's half-sentence about "regenerated by replaying events", the part "confirm that the replay path actually exists and has been rehearsed" held this time only by luck.

### Step 3: Root cause — locks only narrow probability, and the list had no source

Compared against this page's "The real cost of locks: lease, clocks and renewal": the lease was too short, and the lock lapsed before the business finished — of this page's four failure shapes, the first one, "the business execution exceeds the lease duration, a second holder enters, and both sides write at the same time", came true word for word; of renewal threads, release verification and critical-section version checks, not one was implemented, and this page's common pitfall "designing only the success path of acquiring the lock, with no follow-up for lock contention, lock expiry or lock misdeletion" held as well. Compared against "The positioning of cache: an acceleration layer, not a fact layer": the first and most-ignored of the list's four conditions, "the source is explicit, and it can be rebuilt or recovered without relying on the cache", had been answered by nobody — the list existed only inside a Redis set, so the cache turned from an acceleration layer into the de facto authoritative store; this time the clawback could locate individuals only because the event transaction database still existed, not because the list itself was rebuildable.

### Step 4: Disposition and backfill — stack protection on the lock, backstop with idempotency, register the source

The fix came in two parts. Emergency response: alert at **04**:**10**, replay-reconcile at **04**:**25** and identify the double-issued list (reconciliation took **15** minutes), and at **04**:**50** claw back **4,800,000** (80%, unconsumed first); the **1,200,000** already consumed was not chased and was offset into that week's clawback event, with a public notice. Institutional, four steps: long-task locks get a renewal thread plus identity verification before release, and a version check layered inside the critical section; the reward-issuance interface uses "task number + player ID" as its idempotency key, and duplicate requests are deduplicated outright; the Redis set registers "source = event transaction database, rebuildable by replay", and the operations data-pull entry point is moved to the persistence layer; the task's critical section changes from per-call RPC to sharded batch processing plus checkpoint resume, splitting the **60**-minute critical section into **12** segments of **5** minutes each, with the lock held per segment. Recheck: the following week, a rehearsal replays the same list; after idempotency-key deduplication, **24,000** person-entries = **6,000,000** should-issue, zero over-issuance.

**Backfill checklist**:

| Landing point | Action | Backfilled at |
|-----|------|--------|
| Lease governance | Long-task locks get a renewal thread and pre-release verification, plus a version check in the critical section | The real cost of locks: lease, clocks and renewal |
| Idempotency backstop | The reward-issuance interface uses task number + player ID as the idempotency key; duplicate requests deduplicated | What problem does a distributed lock actually solve |
| Source registration | The cache set registers source and rebuild method; the data-pull entry point goes only through the persistence layer | The positioning of cache: an acceleration layer, not a fact layer |
| Reconciliation drill | The compensation task uses ledger replay as the baseline for hourly reconciliation; double issuance alerts immediately | Treating cache as the authoritative source — the cost is usually only settled on outage day |

### Three lessons from the case

1. **A lock's lease is not a deadline, it is a probability** — a 30-minute lease covering a 60-minute task makes a second holder a certainty; most disputes around locks happen at the moment "someone did not get the lock".
2. **A lock only narrows the concurrency window; it cannot stop duplication** — the real line of defense is the idempotency key, cheaper than any layer of lock protection.
3. **A list living in cache only settles the bill on outage day** — with the replay path rehearsed once, reconciliation took **15** minutes; without rehearsal, the only option left would have been to claw back **6,000,000** after the fact.

## Used By

Cache adoption review (four conditions: explicit source, tolerable staleness, frequent enough access, controllable size); leaderboard selection and tiered read paths (snapshot vs rank interface); the decision to introduce a distributed lock (cost of repetition, contents of the critical section, the path for failing to acquire) and lease governance.

- **skynet** (commit `4f76d75`): the dirty work of the cache client concentrates in the channel layer — every store driver (`lualib/skynet/db/redis.lua`, `mysql.lua`, `mongo.lua`) sits on the same `socket_channel.channel` factory (`lualib/skynet/socketchannel.lua:26`): connection and reconnection is `channel:connect` (same file `:474`), request-response pairing by session is `channel:request` (`:510`), and the consumer side gets two dispatch models — dispatch by session (`:96`) and single-threaded in-order dispatch (`:194`). The drivers are left with only protocol encoding and decoding; who is fact, whether to lock, and how consistency is guaranteed are not decided at this layer
